prompt:
currently machine learning things that we have are very generic user
  recommendations to them, i want you to build that in a way that it will scale
  up our recommendations, take these insides from these.
  how much you should sleep / best time, based on data.
  Project health rise that are likely to happen
  Heart health
  analyze daily movement patterns. You could forecast how consistent low
  activity might predict metabolic issues. Use heart rate variability trends to
  anticipate burnout or overtraining risk. You could even integrate dietary
  patterns: “Your glucose spikes correlate with poor sleep; adjusting meals
  might help.” Essentially, map out a 360-degree behavior-health loop, showing
  users how small tweaks in movement, stress, or diet ripple into long-term
  outcomes.
  You can factor in circadian rhythms—not just sleep, but optimal times for
  focus or exercise based on biological patterns. Track recovery speed after
  illness or intense stress, offering tailored recuperation strategies. Detect
  early patterns of chronic issues, nudging them toward preventive care. The
  key is foresight: show them how daily micro-decisions ripple into macro
  health outcomes, giving them a sense of control.
  But rather than just listing, let’s structure your focus. Think categories:
  First, user personalization (sleep, movement, stress, nutrition). Second,
  predictive health insights. Third, behavior nudges. Fourth, data privacy.
  Fifth, user retention strategy.
  Recommend their ideal wind-down routine timing. Two: Detect early fatigue
  patterns before they feel it. Three: Tailor wake-up times to minimize
  grogginess. Four: Suggest ideal meal times for sleep support. Five: Correlate
  stress patterns with sleep disruptions. Six: Offer personalized nap durations
  if needed. Seven: Identify how exercise timing impacts sleep quality. Eight:
  Predict mood patterns based on sleep trends. Nine: Provide early warning of
  potential insomnia risks. Ten: Suggest weekly goals—like one night of
  extended sleep—based on trends. All personalized, all actionable, all showing
  care.
  meetings, screen use, coffee intake. Go hyper-specific. Correlate their
  micro-wake-ups with daily caffeine timing and pinpoint if shifting coffee by
  90 minutes improves sleep continuity. Analyze how their heart rate
  variability changes after specific types of stress—like meetings vs. workouts
  —then deliver a custom recovery protocol. Detect patterns of late-night
  screen use and show the exact melatonin disruption curve. Even relate their
  emotional journaling patterns to physiological rest quality. The more you
  connect their unique habits and signals into precise, actionable
  correlations, the more they’ll feel it’s built just for them.
  Then we craft a lifelong companion. First, detect their unique stress
  triggers—personalize breathwork or micro-breaks before patterns escalate.
  Second, tie their emotional states—via journaling or mood tracking—to
  physical recovery and offer real-time mood interventions. Third, adapt
  activity recommendations based on their unique energy rhythms. Fourth,
  anticipate burnout and suggest preventive actions before they feel it. Fifth,
  personalize micro-diet tweaks, like ideal hydration timing based on their
  HRV. Sixth, warn of early immune system dips, suggesting rest before they get
  sick. Seventh, offer personalized social engagement advice based on recovery
  patterns. Eighth, predict optimal learning or focus times and suggest deep
  work windows. Ninth, detect subtle early signs of chronic conditions and
  guide proactive steps. Tenth, show them how every small habit change tangibly
  shifts their future risk. Make them feel you are their invisible guardian.

  Your ML strategy should evolve in layers. Start simple: build baseline models
  from aggregated patterns—sleep stages, HRV, stress. Then let user data fine-
  tune personalized models. Use transfer learning—start from general population
  patterns, adapt to individual traits. As data scales, consider federated
  learning—personalization on-device to protect privacy while improving global
  models. Think adaptive feedback loops—your app learns from user interactions,
  improving predictions. Finally, keep iterating; early patterns will inform
  future models, making each user’s experience more uniquely accurate over
  time.

  You’ll want a hybrid approach. Begin with a strong base model trained on
  broad patterns. Then, implement on-device personalization—continual fine-
  tuning based on each user’s data. Use online learning—your app dynamically
  updates its model as new user data streams in. Leverage cloud aggregation for
  global insights, while ensuring personalized models stay unique. Regularly
  validate user-level patterns, and flag unique trends that diverge from
  population norms. In short, it’s a constant feedback loop—from general to
  personal, always adapting as the user evolves.

  You’ll want to start with a foundation of time-series models. Use something
  like a long short-term memory (LSTM) network, which can capture sequential
  patterns in health data—like heart rate or sleep trends. Layer in a
  personalization component—for example, a mixture of experts, where a general
  model is combined with a user-specific expert. Implement online learning—so
  each user’s model continues to update with their data. Federate the learning—
  so user data stays on the device, while aggregated insights improve the base
  model. Finally, for unique patterns, use anomaly detection—something like an
  autoencoder—to flag deviations and trigger tailored recommendations. This
  keeps it both scalable and personal. Task 1 — Fix Granger Causality
  Implementation
    Replace the equal-weight averaging in CorrelationDiscovery.swift with
  proper OLS regression using Accelerate's LAPACK
    routines (sgesv/dgesv). The current autoregressiveSSE() method at line 225
  uses series[t - lag] / Double(maxLag) which
    is just a uniform average — not a fitted autoregressive model. Properly fit
  autoregressive coefficients for both the
    restricted model (y lags only) and unrestricted model (y lags + x lags) by
  solving the normal equations X'X*β = X'y.
    Then compute a valid F-statistic from the ratio of SSE reductions. Replace
  approximateFPValue() at line 263 with a
    proper incomplete beta function for the F-distribution CDF (the current
  exponential approximation produces wrong
    p-values). Without this, every Granger causality result is statistically
  meaningless.

    Task 2 — Add Model Evaluation & Logging Framework
    Create an MLEvaluator class that tracks prediction-vs-actual for every ML
  component. For PredictiveScorer: log each
    daily prediction and the next-day outcome, compute rolling accuracy,
  precision, recall, and a calibration curve (10
    bins, predicted probability vs observed frequency). For
  TimeSeriesForecaster: log forecast vs observed per metric,
    compute MAE and MAPE. For HealthStateClassifier: track silhouette score
  trend across retrains. For
    AdaptiveAnomalyDetector: track false positive rate by counting user-
  dismissed anomalies vs total flagged. Store
    evaluation history in a new StoredMLEvaluation SwiftData model with fields:
  componentName, evaluationDate, metricsJSON
    (serialized dictionary of evaluation metrics). Surface a debug/developer
  view (behind a hidden tap gesture in Settings)
     showing model health — accuracy trends, calibration plots, data
  sufficiency per component.

    Task 3 — Ship Pre-Trained Base Models to Kill Cold Start
    Train baseline models offline using Python (scikit-learn / statsmodels) on
  synthetic or population-average health data.
     Export as .mlmodel files for: (a) a logistic regression for bad-day
  prediction with population-average weights, (b)
    clustering centroids for 5 canonical health states (Recovery, Peak
  Performance, Stressed, Under-Slept, Normal), (c)
    baseline Holt-Winters parameters (level, trend, seasonal factors) per
  common metric (HR, HRV, steps, sleep, calories).
    Bundle these .mlmodel files in the app bundle. On first launch, load base
  models immediately so users see predictions
    from day 1. As user data accumulates (past the minimumDays thresholds),
  blend base model predictions with personalized
    model predictions using a confidence-weighted mix: output = (1 -
  userConfidence) * basePrediction + userConfidence *
    personalPrediction where userConfidence ramps from 0 to 1 over the first 60
  days. Remove or shorten all minimumDays
    gates since base models provide day-1 predictions.

    Task 4 — Migrate PredictiveScorer to CoreML with On-Device Personalization
    Replace the hand-rolled logistic regression in PredictiveScorer.swift with
  a CoreML .mlmodel. Use MLUpdateTask for
    on-device fine-tuning with the user's daily data. Define an updatable model
  with a logistic regression or small neural
    net (1 hidden layer, 32 units) in CoreML format — create it using
  coremltools in Python with an MLParameterKey
    configuration for updatable weights. Keep the same feature construction
  (buildFeatureArray) but feed it through
    CoreML's MLFeatureProvider protocol. Persist the personalized model in the
  app's documents directory (Application
    Support). On each daily update, call MLUpdateTask with the latest day's
  features and label. Fallback to the bundled
    base model if personalization hasn't happened yet. Keep the
  extractTopFactors weight×feature attribution logic but read
     weights from the CoreML model parameters.

    Task 5 — Migrate HealthStateClassifier to CoreML
    Replace the hand-rolled K-means++ in HealthStateClassifier.swift with a
  CoreML KNN or nearest-centroid model. Train an
    initial model with Create ML or export from Python using coremltools —
  define a pipeline model with a nearest-neighbor
    classifier and the 5 canonical centroids from Task 3. Use MLUpdateTask to
  re-cluster on-device as new data arrives by
    updating centroid positions. Keep the auto-labeling logic (generateLabel)
  and transition matrix computation as
    post-processing on top of CoreML inference — CoreML handles "which centroid
  is closest" and your code handles "what
    does that centroid mean." Benefit: Neural Engine acceleration and validated
  distance computation. Store the
cation Support alongside the predictive model.

    Task 6 — Migrate Isolation Forest to CoreML Tree Ensemble
    Replace the hand-rolled IsolationNode indirect enum tree in
  AdaptiveAnomalyDetector.swift with a CoreML tree ensemble
    model. Export a trained Isolation Forest from Python (scikit-learn
  IsolationForest →
    coremltools.converters.sklearn.convert) as a .mlmodel. Bundle the base
  forest in the app. For on-device retraining,
    periodically (every 30 days) export user feature vectors to a temporary
  array, rebuild the forest using a background
    Task, and save the updated .mlmodel to Application Support. This also
  solves the persistence problem since CoreML
    models are files on disk — no need to make IsolationNode Codable. Keep the
  contextual peer comparison logic
    (contextualZScore) as a post-processing step on top of the CoreML anomaly
  score.

    Task 7 — Add Monthly and Menstrual Cycle Seasonality to Forecaster
    Extend TimeSeriesForecaster.swift from single-period Holt-Winters
  (period=7) to double seasonal (Holt-Winters with two
    seasonal components). Add a second seasonal array with period=28 to
  HoltWintersState — this captures monthly/menstrual
    patterns. Modify fitWithParams to decompose both weekly and monthly
  seasonality: after removing level and trend, fit
    weekly seasonal factors first, then fit monthly factors on the weekly-
  deseasonalized residuals. Update forecast() to
    multiply both seasonal components: (level + trend * h) * weekSeasonal[h%7]
  * monthSeasonal[h%28]. Add a second gamma
    parameter (gammaMonthly) to the grid search. For users who track menstrual
  cycle data in HealthKit
    (HKCategoryTypeIdentifier.menstrualFlow), use the actual cycle length
  instead of assuming 28 days — query HealthKit for
     the average cycle length and use that as the monthly period. Optionally
  add period=90 for seasonal/quarterly patterns
    if data exceeds 180 days.

    Task 8 — Add Inter-Metric Ratio Features to FeatureEngine
    In FeatureEngine.swift, add composite features after computing per-metric
  features. Define a CompositeFeature enum with
     cases: (a) hrvRhrRatio — HRV divided by resting heart rate (autonomic
  balance indicator, higher = better recovery),
    (b) exerciseIntensity — active calories divided by steps (intensity per
  unit of movement), (c) sleepQuality — sleep
    duration multiplied by deep sleep percentage (composite quality score), (d)
  recoveryIndex — HRV × sleep duration /
    resting heart rate (multi-factor recovery score). For each composite,
  compute the ratio/product from the raw
    (pre-normalized) daily values, then z-score normalize using the same
  Welford machinery. Add new FeatureType cases
    (.composite_hrvRhr, etc.) and append to orderedKeys so all downstream
  consumers (anomaly detector, classifier,
    predictor) automatically see and use these features without any changes to
  their code.

    Task 9 — Add Cumulative Training Load Features
    In FeatureEngine.swift, compute sports-science standard training load
  features. (a) Acute:chronic workload ratio —
    7-day exponentially weighted moving average of active calories divided by
  28-day EWMA. This is the standard ACR from
    the Banister model; values above 1.5 indicate injury/overtraining risk. (b)
  monotoneIndex — count of consecutive days
    where a metric stays above or below baseline (e.g., 5 consecutive days of
  below-baseline HRV is a strong fatigue
    signal). (c) streakFeature — consecutive days hitting the user's daily
  target (steps > baseline, sleep > baseline). Add
     these as new FeatureType cases
  (.acuteChronicRatio, .streakLength, .monotoneIndex). Compute using a lookback
  window
    over the date-indexed data already available in buildFeatureVectors. These
  features require at least 28 days of data to
     be meaningful.

    Task 10 — Add Sleep Timing and Consistency Features
    In FeatureEngine.swift, add features derived from sleep timing (not just
  duration). (a) Bedtime consistency — standard
    deviation of bedtime (sleep onset) over the last 7 days. Lower = more
  consistent = better. (b) Social jet lag —
    difference in average bedtime on weekdays vs weekends. Higher = worse
  circadian disruption. (c) Sleep midpoint — the
    midpoint between sleep onset and wake time, which is a proxy for circadian
  phase. Query
    HKCategoryTypeIdentifier.sleepAnalysis for in-bed start time (not just
  total duration) — this requires a new HealthKit
    query in HealthKitManager that fetches the actual sleep analysis intervals
  rather than the aggregated duration. Add new
     FeatureType cases (.bedtimeConsistency, .socialJetLag, .sleepMidpoint).
  These features are more predictive of next-day
     performance than sleep duration alone according to sleep research.

    Task 11 — Add Weather/Environmental Features via WeatherKit
    Create a WeatherFeatureProvider class that fetches daily weather data from
  Apple's WeatherKit API. Fetch: barometric
    pressure, temperature, humidity, UV index. Store in a new
  StoredWeatherSample SwiftData model with fields: date,
    pressure, temperature, humidity, uvIndex. In FeatureEngine, add a method to
  merge weather features into
    DailyFeatureVector after building health features — add 4 new FeatureType
  cases for weather metrics. Barometric
    pressure is a known correlate of HRV and migraine; temperature affects
  resting heart rate. Gate behind a user
    permission toggle in Settings (WeatherKit requires the WeatherKit
  capability and a privacy description). These are
    contextual features — they don't come from HealthKit and provide external
  explanatory power. The provider should fetch
    historical weather for the user's location using CLLocationManager for
  current coordinates and
    WeatherService.shared.weather(for:including:) for daily history.

    Task 12 — Add Uncertainty Quantification with Conformal Prediction
    Create a ConformalCalibrator class that wraps any point prediction with
  guaranteed coverage intervals. During training,
     collect a calibration set of nonconformity scores — for regression
  (forecaster): |predicted - actual|; for
    classification (predictive scorer): 1 - P(correct class). Store the sorted
  calibration scores. At inference, for a
    desired confidence level (e.g., 90%), compute the quantile q at position
  ceil((1 - alpha) * (n + 1)) / n of the stored
    scores. Report prediction intervals as [prediction - q, prediction + q] for
  regression, and "confident" only if
    P(predicted class) > 1 - q for classification. Apply to
  TimeSeriesForecaster forecasts (replace the current heuristic
    confidenceInterval method) and PredictiveScorer probabilities. Store
  calibration scores in
    StoredMLModelState.parametersJSON. Surface confidence level in the UI —
  only show "high confidence" predictions when
    coverage is above 80%.

    Task 13 — Make Isolation Forest Persistable
    Make IsolationNode and IsolationTree in AdaptiveAnomalyDetector.swift
  Codable. The IsolationNode enum has two cases:
    .branch(featureIndex: Int, splitValue: Double, left: IsolationNode, right:
  IsolationNode) and .leaf(size: Int).
    Implement custom Codable conformance with a type discriminator key
  ("branch" or "leaf") and recursive encoding for the
    tree structure. Add Codable to IsolationTree. Create methods serialize() ->
  Data and static func deserialize(from:
    Data) -> [IsolationTree] for the full forest. Save/restore via
  StoredMLModelState.parametersJSON — on app launch, check
     if a stored forest exists and restore it instead of rebuilding from raw
  feature vectors. Add a version field so stale
    forests (trained with different feature dimensions) trigger a retrain
  instead of crashing. This eliminates the O(n ×
    trees) rebuild cost on every cold start. Skip this task if doing Task 6
  (CoreML migration) since CoreML models persist
    as files automatically.

    Task 14 — Add Prophet-Style Multi-Seasonal Decomposition
    Create a SeasonalDecomposer class as an alternative/upgrade to
  TimeSeriesForecaster. Implement additive decomposition:
    y(t) = trend(t) + weekly(t) + monthly(t) + seasonal(t) + residual(t). For
  trend extraction, use iterative LOESS
    (locally weighted regression) — implement LOESS with a tricube kernel and
  locally fitted linear regression at each
    point, using a bandwidth of ~20% of the data. For seasonal components, fit
  Fourier series (sin/cos pairs) at the known
    periodicities: weekly (period 7: 3 Fourier terms), monthly (period 28-30: 2
  terms), seasonal (period 90: 2 terms). This
     is the same approach Facebook Prophet uses internally. Solve the Fourier
  coefficients via least squares on the
    trend-removed residuals. This handles multiple overlapping periodicities
  better than multiplicative Holt-Winters. Can
    coexist with the existing forecaster — use decomposer for generating
  seasonal insights ("your HRV peaks in spring"),
    use the forecaster for point predictions.

    Task 15 — Add Temporal Fusion Transformer via CoreML
    Train a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) in Python (PyTorch) on synthetic
  multi-metric health data. The TFT
    architecture handles: variable-length inputs, multi-horizon forecasting (1-
  7 days ahead), and provides built-in
    attention-based feature importance via its Variable Selection Network and
  Interpretable Multi-Head Attention layers.
    Generate synthetic training data that mimics realistic health patterns —
  weekly cycles, menstrual cycles, gradual
    trends, random anomalies, correlated metrics (HRV inversely correlated with
  RHR). Export the trained model to CoreML
    format via coremltools.convert(). Bundle as a .mlmodel in the app. Use for
  7-day-ahead multi-metric forecasting. The
    attention weights from the model directly explain "why" a prediction was
  made — they tell you which past time steps and
     which metrics most influenced the forecast. This replaces the manual
  extractTopFactors heuristic in PredictiveScorer
    with learned, data-driven attribution. This is the most advanced
  forecasting architecture that runs efficiently on
    Apple Neural Engine.

    Task 16 — Add Ensemble Disagreement for Epistemic Uncertainty
    In MLOrchestrator.swift, add an ensemble uncertainty module that combines
  predictions from multiple independent models
    (forecaster, anomaly detector, predictive scorer) to estimate epistemic
  uncertainty. When models agree (all flag
    anomaly, or all say normal), confidence is high. When models disagree
  (forecaster says normal, isolation forest says
    anomaly, predictive scorer says 50/50), flag as uncertain — present to the
  user as "we're not sure about this one."
    Implement as a voting mechanism across components: for each day, count how
  many models flag it as concerning.
    ensembleConfidence = agreementRatio × min(componentConfidences) where
  agreementRatio is the fraction of models that
    agree on the direction. Add an UncertaintyLevel enum (.high, .medium, .low)
  to MLPrediction. Only surface insights with
     medium+ confidence. This prevents overconfident single-model predictions
  from alarming users.

    Task 17 — Add MC Dropout Uncertainty for Neural Models
    If using CoreML neural net models (from Tasks 4 or 15), implement Monte
  Carlo Dropout at inference time. MC Dropout
    means running the same input through the model N times (e.g., 20) with
  dropout layers active (not disabled as in
    standard inference), then collecting the distribution of outputs. The
  variance of outputs estimates model uncertainty —
     high variance means the model is unsure (out-of-distribution input), low
  variance means confident. In CoreML, this
    requires setting the model's dropout layers to remain active during
  inference — create a custom MLModel subclass or use
     MLModelConfiguration to enable training mode during prediction. Compute
  mean(outputs) as the prediction and
    std(outputs) as the uncertainty. Map standard deviation to a confidence
  score: confidence = 1 / (1 + std). Surface as a
     calibrated confidence score alongside each prediction in the UI. Only
  applicable to neural network models — skip for
    logistic regression or tree-based models.

    Task 18 — Add Calibration Curves and Platt Scaling to PredictiveScorer
    After training the logistic regression (or CoreML equivalent) in
  PredictiveScorer, hold out a calibration set (last 20%
     of training data). Plot predicted probability vs observed frequency in 10
  bins — if bin 0.7-0.8 has predicted
    probability 0.75 but only 40% of those days were actually bad, the model is
  overconfident. If the model is
    miscalibrated, apply Platt scaling — fit a secondary sigmoid P_calibrated =
  1/(1+exp(A*logit + B)) on the calibration
    set using maximum likelihood (gradient descent on the log-likelihood).
  Store A and B as parameters alongside the model
    weights. At inference time, pass the raw logit through the Platt sigmoid
  before reporting the probability. This ensures
     when the model tells the user "80% chance of a bad day tomorrow," it
  actually happens roughly 80% of the time.
    Critical for user trust. Add a CalibrationState struct with (A, B,
  binAccuracies) to StoredMLModelState for
    persistence. Run recalibration every 30 days alongside model retraining."

    clustering centroids for 5 canonical health states (Recovery, Peak
  Performance, Stressed, Under-Slept, Normal), (c)
    baseline Holt-Winters parameters (level, trend, seasonal factors) per
  common metric (HR, HRV, steps, sleep, calories).
    Bundle these .mlmodel files in the app bundle. On first launch, load base
  models immediately so users see predictions
    from day 1. As user data accumulates (past the minimumDays thresholds),
  blend base model predictions with personalized
    model predictions using a confidence-weighted mix: output = (1 -
  userConfidence) * basePrediction + userConfidence *
    personalPrediction where userConfidence ramps from 0 to 1 over the first 60
  days. Remove or shorten all minimumDays
    gates since base models provide day-1 predictions.

    Task 4 — Migrate PredictiveScorer to CoreML with On-Device Personalization
    Replace the hand-rolled logistic regression in PredictiveScorer.swift with
  a CoreML .mlmodel. Use MLUpdateTask for
    on-device fine-tuning with the user's daily data. Define an updatable model
  with a logistic regression or small neural
    net (1 hidden layer, 32 units) in CoreML format — create it using
  coremltools in Python with an MLParameterKey
    configuration for updatable weights. Keep the same feature construction
  (buildFeatureArray) but feed it through
    CoreML's MLFeatureProvider protocol. Persist the personalized model in the
  app's documents directory (Application
    Support). On each daily update, call MLUpdateTask with the latest day's
  features and label. Fallback to the bundled
    base model if personalization hasn't happened yet. Keep the
  extractTopFactors weight×feature attribution logic but read
     weights from the CoreML model parameters.

    Task 5 — Migrate HealthStateClassifier to CoreML
    Replace the hand-rolled K-means++ in HealthStateClassifier.swift with a
  CoreML KNN or nearest-centroid model. Train an
    initial model with Create ML or export from Python using coremltools —
  define a pipeline model with a nearest-neighbor
    classifier and the 5 canonical centroids from Task 3. Use MLUpdateTask to
  re-cluster on-device as new data arrives by
    updating centroid positions. Keep the auto-labeling logic (generateLabel)
  and transition matrix computation as
    post-processing on top of CoreML inference — CoreML handles "which centroid
  is closest" and your code handles "what
    does that centroid mean." Benefit: Neural Engine acceleration and validated
  distance computation. Store the
cation Support alongside the predictive model.

    Task 6 — Migrate Isolation Forest to CoreML Tree Ensemble
    Replace the hand-rolled IsolationNode indirect enum tree in
  AdaptiveAnomalyDetector.swift with a CoreML tree ensemble
    model. Export a trained Isolation Forest from Python (scikit-learn
  IsolationForest →
    coremltools.converters.sklearn.convert) as a .mlmodel. Bundle the base
  forest in the app. For on-device retraining,
    periodically (every 30 days) export user feature vectors to a temporary
  array, rebuild the forest using a background
    Task, and save the updated .mlmodel to Application Support. This also
  solves the persistence problem since CoreML
    models are files on disk — no need to make IsolationNode Codable. Keep the
  contextual peer comparison logic
    (contextualZScore) as a post-processing step on top of the CoreML anomaly
  score.

    Task 7 — Add Monthly and Menstrual Cycle Seasonality to Forecaster
    Extend TimeSeriesForecaster.swift from single-period Holt-Winters
  (period=7) to double seasonal (Holt-Winters with two
    seasonal components). Add a second seasonal array with period=28 to
  HoltWintersState — this captures monthly/menstrual
    patterns. Modify fitWithParams to decompose both weekly and monthly
  seasonality: after removing level and trend, fit
    weekly seasonal factors first, then fit monthly factors on the weekly-
  deseasonalized residuals. Update forecast() to
    multiply both seasonal components: (level + trend * h) * weekSeasonal[h%7]
  * monthSeasonal[h%28]. Add a second gamma
    parameter (gammaMonthly) to the grid search. For users who track menstrual
  cycle data in HealthKit
    (HKCategoryTypeIdentifier.menstrualFlow), use the actual cycle length
  instead of assuming 28 days — query HealthKit for
     the average cycle length and use that as the monthly period. Optionally
  add period=90 for seasonal/quarterly patterns
    if data exceeds 180 days.

    Task 8 — Add Inter-Metric Ratio Features to FeatureEngine
    In FeatureEngine.swift, add composite features after computing per-metric
  features. Define a CompositeFeature enum with
     cases: (a) hrvRhrRatio — HRV divided by resting heart rate (autonomic
  balance indicator, higher = better recovery),
    (b) exerciseIntensity — active calories divided by steps (intensity per
  unit of movement), (c) sleepQuality — sleep
    duration multiplied by deep sleep percentage (composite quality score), (d)
  recoveryIndex — HRV × sleep duration /
    resting heart rate (multi-factor recovery score). For each composite,
  compute the ratio/product from the raw
    (pre-normalized) daily values, then z-score normalize using the same
  Welford machinery. Add new FeatureType cases
    (.composite_hrvRhr, etc.) and append to orderedKeys so all downstream
  consumers (anomaly detector, classifier,
    predictor) automatically see and use these features without any changes to
  their code.

    Task 9 — Add Cumulative Training Load Features
    In FeatureEngine.swift, compute sports-science standard training load
  features. (a) Acute:chronic workload ratio —
    7-day exponentially weighted moving average of active calories divided by
  28-day EWMA. This is the standard ACR from
    the Banister model; values above 1.5 indicate injury/overtraining risk. (b)
  monotoneIndex — count of consecutive days
    where a metric stays above or below baseline (e.g., 5 consecutive days of
  below-baseline HRV is a strong fatigue
    signal). (c) streakFeature — consecutive days hitting the user's daily
  target (steps > baseline, sleep > baseline). Add
     these as new FeatureType cases
  (.acuteChronicRatio, .streakLength, .monotoneIndex). Compute using a lookback
  window
    over the date-indexed data already available in buildFeatureVectors. These
  features require at least 28 days of data to
     be meaningful.

    Task 10 — Add Sleep Timing and Consistency Features
    In FeatureEngine.swift, add features derived from sleep timing (not just
  duration). (a) Bedtime consistency — standard
    deviation of bedtime (sleep onset) over the last 7 days. Lower = more
  consistent = better. (b) Social jet lag —
    difference in average bedtime on weekdays vs weekends. Higher = worse
  circadian disruption. (c) Sleep midpoint — the
    midpoint between sleep onset and wake time, which is a proxy for circadian
  phase. Query
    HKCategoryTypeIdentifier.sleepAnalysis for in-bed start time (not just
  total duration) — this requires a new HealthKit
    query in HealthKitManager that fetches the actual sleep analysis intervals
  rather than the aggregated duration. Add new
     FeatureType cases (.bedtimeConsistency, .socialJetLag, .sleepMidpoint).
  These features are more predictive of next-day
     performance than sleep duration alone according to sleep research.

    Task 11 — Add Weather/Environmental Features via WeatherKit
    Create a WeatherFeatureProvider class that fetches daily weather data from
  Apple's WeatherKit API. Fetch: barometric
    pressure, temperature, humidity, UV index. Store in a new
  StoredWeatherSample SwiftData model with fields: date,
    pressure, temperature, humidity, uvIndex. In FeatureEngine, add a method to
  merge weather features into
    DailyFeatureVector after building health features — add 4 new FeatureType
  cases for weather metrics. Barometric
    pressure is a known correlate of HRV and migraine; temperature affects
  resting heart rate. Gate behind a user
    permission toggle in Settings (WeatherKit requires the WeatherKit
  capability and a privacy description). These are
    contextual features — they don't come from HealthKit and provide external
  explanatory power. The provider should fetch
    historical weather for the user's location using CLLocationManager for
  current coordinates and
    WeatherService.shared.weather(for:including:) for daily history.

    Task 12 — Add Uncertainty Quantification with Conformal Prediction
    Create a ConformalCalibrator class that wraps any point prediction with
  guaranteed coverage intervals. During training,
     collect a calibration set of nonconformity scores — for regression
  (forecaster): |predicted - actual|; for
    classification (predictive scorer): 1 - P(correct class). Store the sorted
  calibration scores. At inference, for a
    desired confidence level (e.g., 90%), compute the quantile q at position
  ceil((1 - alpha) * (n + 1)) / n of the stored
    scores. Report prediction intervals as [prediction - q, prediction + q] for
  regression, and "confident" only if
    P(predicted class) > 1 - q for classification. Apply to
  TimeSeriesForecaster forecasts (replace the current heuristic
    confidenceInterval method) and PredictiveScorer probabilities. Store
  calibration scores in
    StoredMLModelState.parametersJSON. Surface confidence level in the UI —
  only show "high confidence" predictions when
    coverage is above 80%.

    Task 13 — Make Isolation Forest Persistable
    Make IsolationNode and IsolationTree in AdaptiveAnomalyDetector.swift
  Codable. The IsolationNode enum has two cases:
    .branch(featureIndex: Int, splitValue: Double, left: IsolationNode, right:
  IsolationNode) and .leaf(size: Int).
    Implement custom Codable conformance with a type discriminator key
  ("branch" or "leaf") and recursive encoding for the
    tree structure. Add Codable to IsolationTree. Create methods serialize() ->
  Data and static func deserialize(from:
    Data) -> [IsolationTree] for the full forest. Save/restore via
  StoredMLModelState.parametersJSON — on app launch, check
     if a stored forest exists and restore it instead of rebuilding from raw
  feature vectors. Add a version field so stale
    forests (trained with different feature dimensions) trigger a retrain
  instead of crashing. This eliminates the O(n ×
    trees) rebuild cost on every cold start. Skip this task if doing Task 6
  (CoreML migration) since CoreML models persist
    as files automatically.

    Task 14 — Add Prophet-Style Multi-Seasonal Decomposition
    Create a SeasonalDecomposer class as an alternative/upgrade to
  TimeSeriesForecaster. Implement additive decomposition:
    y(t) = trend(t) + weekly(t) + monthly(t) + seasonal(t) + residual(t). For
  trend extraction, use iterative LOESS
    (locally weighted regression) — implement LOESS with a tricube kernel and
  locally fitted linear regression at each
    point, using a bandwidth of ~20% of the data. For seasonal components, fit
  Fourier series (sin/cos pairs) at the known
    periodicities: weekly (period 7: 3 Fourier terms), monthly (period 28-30: 2
  terms), seasonal (period 90: 2 terms). This
     is the same approach Facebook Prophet uses internally. Solve the Fourier
  coefficients via least squares on the
    trend-removed residuals. This handles multiple overlapping periodicities
  better than multiplicative Holt-Winters. Can
    coexist with the existing forecaster — use decomposer for generating
  seasonal insights ("your HRV peaks in spring"),
    use the forecaster for point predictions.

    Task 15 — Add Temporal Fusion Transformer via CoreML
    Train a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) in Python (PyTorch) on synthetic
  multi-metric health data. The TFT
    architecture handles: variable-length inputs, multi-horizon forecasting (1-
  7 days ahead), and provides built-in
    attention-based feature importance via its Variable Selection Network and
  Interpretable Multi-Head Attention layers.
    Generate synthetic training data that mimics realistic health patterns —
  weekly cycles, menstrual cycles, gradual
    trends, random anomalies, correlated metrics (HRV inversely correlated with
  RHR). Export the trained model to CoreML
    format via coremltools.convert(). Bundle as a .mlmodel in the app. Use for
  7-day-ahead multi-metric forecasting. The
    attention weights from the model directly explain "why" a prediction was
  made — they tell you which past time steps and
     which metrics most influenced the forecast. This replaces the manual
  extractTopFactors heuristic in PredictiveScorer
    with learned, data-driven attribution. This is the most advanced
  forecasting architecture that runs efficiently on
    Apple Neural Engine.

    Task 16 — Add Ensemble Disagreement for Epistemic Uncertainty
    In MLOrchestrator.swift, add an ensemble uncertainty module that combines
  predictions from multiple independent models
    (forecaster, anomaly detector, predictive scorer) to estimate epistemic
  uncertainty. When models agree (all flag
    anomaly, or all say normal), confidence is high. When models disagree
  (forecaster says normal, isolation forest says
    anomaly, predictive scorer says 50/50), flag as uncertain — present to the
  user as "we're not sure about this one."
    Implement as a voting mechanism across components: for each day, count how
  many models flag it as concerning.
    ensembleConfidence = agreementRatio × min(componentConfidences) where
  agreementRatio is the fraction of models that
    agree on the direction. Add an UncertaintyLevel enum (.high, .medium, .low)
  to MLPrediction. Only surface insights with
     medium+ confidence. This prevents overconfident single-model predictions
  from alarming users.

    Task 17 — Add MC Dropout Uncertainty for Neural Models
    If using CoreML neural net models (from Tasks 4 or 15), implement Monte
  Carlo Dropout at inference time. MC Dropout
    means running the same input through the model N times (e.g., 20) with
  dropout layers active (not disabled as in
    standard inference), then collecting the distribution of outputs. The
  variance of outputs estimates model uncertainty —
     high variance means the model is unsure (out-of-distribution input), low
  variance means confident. In CoreML, this
    requires setting the model's dropout layers to remain active during
  inference — create a custom MLModel subclass or use
     MLModelConfiguration to enable training mode during prediction. Compute
  mean(outputs) as the prediction and
    std(outputs) as the uncertainty. Map standard deviation to a confidence
  score: confidence = 1 / (1 + std). Surface as a
     calibrated confidence score alongside each prediction in the UI. Only
  applicable to neural network models — skip for
    logistic regression or tree-based models.

    Task 18 — Add Calibration Curves and Platt Scaling to PredictiveScorer
    After training the logistic regression (or CoreML equivalent) in
  PredictiveScorer, hold out a calibration set (last 20%
     of training data). Plot predicted probability vs observed frequency in 10
  bins — if bin 0.7-0.8 has predicted
    probability 0.75 but only 40% of those days were actually bad, the model is
  overconfident. If the model is
    miscalibrated, apply Platt scaling — fit a secondary sigmoid P_calibrated =
  1/(1+exp(A*logit + B)) on the calibration
    set using maximum likelihood (gradient descent on the log-likelihood).
  Store A and B as parameters alongside the model
    weights. At inference time, pass the raw logit through the Platt sigmoid
  before reporting the probability. This ensures
     when the model tells the user "80% chance of a bad day tomorrow," it
  actually happens roughly 80% of the time.
    Critical for user trust. Add a CalibrationState struct with (A, B,
  binAccuracies) to StoredMLModelState for
    persistence. Run recalibration every 30 days alongside model retraining.

tasks.title: Fix Granger Causality with proper OLS regression and F-test
tasks.spec: In CorrelationDiscovery.swift, replace the autoregressiveSSE() method (~line 225) which uses uniform averaging (series[t - lag] / Double(maxLag)) with proper OLS regression. Build design matrices for the restricted model (y lags only) and unrestricted model (y lags + x lags). Solve normal equations X'X*β = X'y using Accelerate's LAPACK dgesv routine. Compute SSE for both models. Calculate F-statistic = ((SSE_restricted - SSE_unrestricted) / numRestrictions) / (SSE_unrestricted / (n - numParams)). Replace approximateFPValue() (~line 263) with a proper incomplete beta function (regularized) for the F-distribution CDF: P(F > f) = I_x(d2/2, d1/2) where x = d2/(d2 + d1*f). Implement the regularized incomplete beta function using a continued fraction expansion (Lentz's algorithm) for numerical stability. Import Accelerate at the top of the file.

tasks.title: Add ML model evaluation and logging framework
tasks.spec: Create MLEvaluator.swift with a class that tracks prediction-vs-actual for all ML components. Implement: (1) For PredictiveScorer: log daily prediction probability and next-day boolean outcome, compute rolling accuracy/precision/recall over a 30-day window, build calibration curve with 10 bins (predicted probability vs observed frequency). (2) For TimeSeriesForecaster: log forecast vs observed per metric, compute MAE and MAPE. (3) For HealthStateClassifier: track silhouette score after each retrain. (4) For AdaptiveAnomalyDetector: track false positive rate (user-dismissed / total flagged). Create StoredMLEvaluation SwiftData model with fields: componentName (String), evaluationDate (Date), metricsJSON (String — serialized [String: Double] dictionary). Create MLModelHealthView.swift — a debug SwiftUI view showing accuracy trends as line charts, calibration plots, and data sufficiency per component. Gate this view behind a hidden gesture (5-tap on the Settings version label). Add navigation to it from Settings.

tasks.title: Train and export pre-trained base CoreML models for cold start
tasks.spec: Create a Python directory (Scripts/train_base_models/) with training scripts. (a) train_bad_day_predictor.py: Generate synthetic health data (1000 users × 365 days) with realistic distributions for HR (60-100), HRV (20-80ms), steps (2000-15000), sleep (4-10h), calories (1500-3500). Label 'bad days' using heuristics (low HRV + poor sleep + high RHR). Train a logistic regression with scikit-learn. Export to CoreML using coremltools with updatable=True and MLParameterKey configuration for weights and bias. Save as BaseBadDayPredictor.mlmodel. (b) train_health_state_centroids.py: Cluster the synthetic data into 5 states (Recovery, PeakPerformance, Stressed, UnderSlept, Normal) using K-means. Export as a nearest-neighbor classifier .mlmodel with the 5 centroids. Save as BaseHealthStateClassifier.mlmodel. (c) train_isolation_forest.py: Train scikit-learn IsolationForest on the synthetic feature vectors. Convert using coremltools.converters.sklearn.convert(). Save as BaseAnomalyDetector.mlmodel. (d) train_holt_winters.py: Fit Holt-Winters (statsmodels) per metric on synthetic time series, export parameters as a JSON file (BaseHoltWintersParams.json) to bundle. Add a requirements.txt (scikit-learn, coremltools, statsmodels, numpy, pandas). Add all .mlmodel files to the Xcode project's Resources group.

tasks.title: Migrate PredictiveScorer to CoreML with on-device personalization
tasks.spec: In PredictiveScorer.swift, replace the hand-rolled logistic regression with CoreML inference. On init, load BaseBadDayPredictor.mlmodel from the app bundle as the base model. Check Application Support for a personalized model file (PersonalizedBadDayPredictor.mlmodel) — if it exists, load that instead. Create an MLFeatureProvider subclass (DailyHealthFeatureProvider) that wraps the existing buildFeatureArray() output into named MLFeatureValue entries matching the model's input schema. For prediction, call model.prediction(from: featureProvider). Implement on-device fine-tuning: after each daily update, create an MLUpdateTask with the latest day's features as input and the actual outcome as the training label. On completion, save the updated model to Application Support. Implement cold-start blending: compute userConfidence = min(1.0, Double(daysOfData) / 60.0). Final prediction = (1 - userConfidence) * basePrediction + userConfidence * personalPrediction. For extractTopFactors, read weights from the CoreML model using model.parameterValue(for: MLParameterKey.weights) and compute weight × feature attribution. Remove or reduce minimumDays gates since the base model provides day-1 predictions.

tasks.title: Migrate HealthStateClassifier to CoreML nearest-centroid model
tasks.spec: In HealthStateClassifier.swift, replace the hand-rolled K-means++ with CoreML inference. Load BaseHealthStateClassifier.mlmodel from the bundle on init. Check Application Support for a personalized version. Create an MLFeatureProvider for the daily feature vector. For classification, call model.prediction() to get the nearest centroid/cluster assignment. Keep the existing generateLabel() logic as post-processing — CoreML returns a cluster index, your code maps it to a meaningful label (Recovery, PeakPerformance, Stressed, UnderSlept, Normal). Keep the transition matrix computation as-is — it operates on classified states, not on the model internals. For on-device re-clustering, use MLUpdateTask periodically (every 14 days when sufficient new data exists) to update centroid positions. Save updated model to Application Support. Implement the same userConfidence blending as PredictiveScorer for cold-start. Remove minimumDays gates.

tasks.title: Migrate Isolation Forest to CoreML tree ensemble
tasks.spec: In AdaptiveAnomalyDetector.swift, replace the hand-rolled IsolationNode indirect enum tree with CoreML inference. Load BaseAnomalyDetector.mlmodel from the bundle. For anomaly scoring, create an MLFeatureProvider from the feature vector and call model.prediction() to get the anomaly score. Keep the contextualZScore() peer comparison logic as a post-processing step on top of the CoreML anomaly score. For on-device retraining: every 30 days, collect all user feature vectors from the last 90 days into an array, dispatch to a background Task that rebuilds the isolation forest in Python-exported format (or use a simple on-device retrain by re-exporting). Save the updated .mlmodel to Application Support. Remove the IsolationNode enum, IsolationTree struct, and all manual tree-building code (buildTree, pathLength, etc.) since CoreML handles this. This also solves persistence — no need for Codable conformance since .mlmodel files persist on disk. Keep the anomaly threshold logic and user-feedback dismiss tracking.

tasks.title: Add monthly and menstrual cycle seasonality to Holt-Winters forecaster
tasks.spec: In TimeSeriesForecaster.swift, extend HoltWintersState to support double seasonality. Add a second seasonal array monthSeasonal with period=28 alongside the existing weekSeasonal (period=7). Add a gammaMonthly smoothing parameter. In fitWithParams(), after computing level and trend, fit weekly seasonal factors first (existing logic), then fit monthly factors on the weekly-deseasonalized residuals. Update the smoothing equations: after updating weekly seasonal, compute the monthly residual and update monthSeasonal[t % monthPeriod] using gammaMonthly. In forecast(), combine both: prediction = (level + trend * h) * weekSeasonal[h % 7] * monthSeasonal[h % monthPeriod]. Expand the grid search to include gammaMonthly in [0.05, 0.1, 0.2]. Add a HealthKit query for HKCategoryTypeIdentifier.menstrualFlow — if the user tracks menstrual cycles, compute the average cycle length from the last 6 cycles and use that as monthPeriod instead of defaulting to 28. If data exceeds 180 days, optionally add a third seasonal component with period=90 for quarterly patterns. Add a third gamma (gammaSeasonal) and seasonal array for this.

tasks.title: Add composite inter-metric ratio features to FeatureEngine
tasks.spec: In FeatureEngine.swift, add composite feature computation after the existing per-metric feature loop in buildFeatureVectors(). Define new FeatureType enum cases: .composite_hrvRhr, .composite_exerciseIntensity, .composite_sleepQuality, .composite_recoveryIndex. For each day's raw (pre-normalized) values, compute: (a) hrvRhrRatio = HRV / restingHeartRate (autonomic balance; higher = better recovery), (b) exerciseIntensity = activeCalories / max(steps, 1) (intensity per movement unit), (c) sleepQuality = sleepDuration * deepSleepPercentage (composite quality), (d) recoveryIndex = (HRV * sleepDuration) / max(restingHeartRate, 1) (multi-factor recovery). Handle division-by-zero with max(denominator, 1) or a small epsilon. After computing raw composite values across all days, z-score normalize each using the same Welford online statistics machinery already used for per-metric features. Append the 4 new FeatureType cases to orderedKeys so downstream consumers (anomaly detector, classifier, predictor) automatically pick them up.

tasks.title: Add acute:chronic workload ratio and streak features to FeatureEngine
tasks.spec: In FeatureEngine.swift, after the composite feature block (added in inter-metric-ratio-features), add cumulative training load features. Add new FeatureType cases: .acuteChronicRatio, .streakLength, .monotoneIndex. Implementation: (a) Acute:chronic workload ratio — compute 7-day EWMA and 28-day EWMA of activeCalories using the formula ewma[t] = alpha * value[t] + (1 - alpha) * ewma[t-1] where alpha_7 = 2/(7+1) and alpha_28 = 2/(28+1). ACR = ewma7 / max(ewma28, 1). Values > 1.5 indicate overtraining risk. (b) monotoneIndex — for each metric (HRV, steps, sleep), count consecutive days the metric stays above or below its rolling 14-day mean. Take the max across metrics. (c) streakLength — count consecutive days where steps > user's 30-day average AND sleep > user's 30-day average. These features use a lookback window over the date-indexed data already in buildFeatureVectors. Gate behind a minimum of 28 days of data — output 0.0 for all three features if insufficient data. Z-score normalize using Welford. Append to orderedKeys after the composite features.

tasks.title: Add sleep timing and consistency features with HealthKit sleep analysis
tasks.spec: Two files to modify. (1) In HealthKitManager.swift, add a new method fetchSleepIntervals(from:to:) that queries HKCategoryTypeIdentifier.sleepAnalysis for individual sleep analysis samples (not aggregated duration). Return an array of (startDate: Date, endDate: Date, value: HKCategoryValueSleepAnalysis) tuples. Filter for .inBed or .asleepUnspecified/.asleepCore/.asleepDeep/.asleepREM categories. Group by night (samples between 6PM and 12PM next day belong to the same night). For each night, extract sleepOnset (earliest inBed/asleep start) and wakeTime (latest asleep end). (2) In FeatureEngine.swift, after training load features, add new FeatureType cases: .bedtimeConsistency, .socialJetLag, .sleepMidpoint. Consume the sleep intervals from HealthKitManager. Compute: (a) bedtimeConsistency = stddev of sleepOnset times (as minutes-since-midnight) over last 7 days. (b) socialJetLag = abs(mean weekday bedtime - mean weekend bedtime) in minutes. (c) sleepMidpoint = (sleepOnset + wakeTime) / 2 as minutes-since-midnight, per day. Z-score normalize and append to orderedKeys.

tasks.title: Add weather/environmental features via WeatherKit
tasks.spec: Create WeatherFeatureProvider.swift: a class that fetches daily weather data from Apple WeatherKit. Use CLLocationManager to get the user's current coordinates (request whenInUse authorization). Call WeatherService.shared.weather(for: location, including: .daily) to fetch daily weather. Extract: barometricPressure (hPa), temperature (°C mean), humidity (%), uvIndex. Create StoredWeatherSample SwiftData model with fields: date (Date), pressure (Double), temperature (Double), humidity (Double), uvIndex (Double). Cache fetched weather in SwiftData to avoid redundant API calls. Fetch historical weather for the past 90 days on first run, then fetch daily going forward. In FeatureEngine.swift, after sleep timing features, add a method mergeWeatherFeatures(weatherSamples:, into: inout [DailyFeatureVector]). Match weather samples to feature vectors by date. Add 4 new FeatureType cases: .weather_pressure, .weather_temperature, .weather_humidity, .weather_uvIndex. Z-score normalize. Gate behind a user toggle in Settings (add a weatherFeaturesEnabled UserDefaults bool). Add WeatherKit capability to the Xcode project entitlements and a privacy description string.

tasks.title: Add conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification
tasks.spec: Create ConformalCalibrator.swift with a generic class that wraps point predictions with coverage-guaranteed intervals. Two modes: (1) Regression mode (for TimeSeriesForecaster): During calibration, collect nonconformity scores = |predicted - actual| from a held-out calibration set (last 20% of training data). Sort scores. At inference for confidence level alpha (default 0.1 for 90% coverage), compute quantile q at position ceil((1 - alpha) * (n + 1)) / n in the sorted scores. Report intervals as [prediction - q, prediction + q]. (2) Classification mode (for PredictiveScorer): nonconformity score = 1 - P(correct class). At inference, flag 'confident' only if P(predicted class) > 1 - q. Store calibration scores as a sorted [Double] array in StoredMLModelState.parametersJSON under the key 'conformalScores'. In TimeSeriesForecaster.swift, replace the existing heuristic confidenceInterval method with a call to ConformalCalibrator.regressionInterval(). In PredictiveScorer.swift, add a conformalConfident boolean to the prediction output using ConformalCalibrator.isConfident(). Recalibrate every 30 days when models retrain. Add a ConfidenceLevel enum to MLPrediction: .high (>90% coverage), .medium (>80%), .low (<80%). Only show 'high confidence' predictions prominently in the UI.

tasks.title: Add Prophet-style multi-seasonal decomposition
tasks.spec: Create SeasonalDecomposer.swift with a class implementing additive decomposition: y(t) = trend(t) + weekly(t) + monthly(t) + seasonal(t) + residual(t). (1) Trend extraction: Implement LOESS (locally weighted regression) with a tricube kernel K(u) = (1 - |u|³)³ for |u| < 1. At each point t, fit a local linear regression using data within a bandwidth window of ~20% of total data points. Weight each neighbor by the tricube kernel based on distance. Solve the 2x2 weighted least squares system for intercept and slope. Use 2 iterations of robustness reweighting (downweight outliers by bisquare function on residuals). (2) Seasonal components: On the detrended residuals, fit Fourier series at known periodicities. Weekly (period 7): 3 sin/cos pairs → 6 coefficients. Monthly (period 28): 2 pairs → 4 coefficients. Quarterly (period 90): 2 pairs → 4 coefficients if data > 180 days. Build the Fourier design matrix X where X[t, 2k] = sin(2π(k+1)t/period) and X[t, 2k+1] = cos(2π(k+1)t/period). Solve all Fourier coefficients simultaneously via least squares (X'X)^{-1} X'y using Accelerate. (3) Residual = y - trend - sum(seasonal components). Expose methods: decompose(series:) → DecompositionResult with .trend, .weekly, .monthly, .seasonal, .residual arrays. Also expose seasonalInsight() → String that generates user-facing insights like 'Your HRV peaks on Tuesdays and dips in winter months.' This class coexists with TimeSeriesForecaster — use decomposer for insights, forecaster for point predictions.

tasks.title: Train and export Temporal Fusion Transformer for multi-metric forecasting
tasks.spec: Create Scripts/train_tft/ directory. (1) generate_synthetic_data.py: Generate synthetic multi-metric health data for 5000 virtual users × 365 days. Metrics: HR, HRV, steps, sleep, calories, RHR. Include: weekly cycles (lower activity weekends), menstrual cycles (28-day HRV variation for ~50% of users), gradual fitness trends, random anomalies (illness = elevated RHR + low HRV for 3-5 days), correlated metrics (HRV inversely correlated with RHR, r=-0.6). Output as parquet files. (2) train_tft.py: Implement a simplified TFT in PyTorch. Architecture: Variable Selection Network (linear + softmax gating per feature), LSTM encoder (2 layers, 64 hidden), Interpretable Multi-Head Attention (4 heads), and linear output heads for 1-7 day ahead forecasts per metric. Train with L2 loss on multi-horizon targets. Use the synthetic data, 80/20 train/val split. Train for 50 epochs with Adam, lr=1e-3, batch_size=64. (3) export_to_coreml.py: Convert the trained PyTorch model to CoreML using coremltools.convert() with inputs spec matching the feature vector shape (7 days × N metrics). Ensure the attention weights are exposed as an output — add a second output head that returns the attention matrix. Save as TemporalFusionTransformer.mlmodel. (4) In the iOS app, create TFTForecaster.swift that loads the .mlmodel, runs 7-day-ahead multi-metric forecasting, and extracts attention weights for feature attribution. The attention weights replace the manual extractTopFactors heuristic — they tell you which past time steps and which metrics most influenced the forecast.

tasks.title: Add ensemble disagreement for epistemic uncertainty estimation
tasks.spec: In MLOrchestrator.swift, add an ensemble uncertainty module after all individual model predictions are computed. Create an UncertaintyLevel enum: .high, .medium, .low in a new file UncertaintyLevel.swift (or add to MLPrediction.swift if it exists). For each day, collect signals from: (1) PredictiveScorer probability (>0.6 = concerning), (2) AdaptiveAnomalyDetector anomaly flag (boolean), (3) TimeSeriesForecaster deviation from forecast (>1.5 stddev = concerning). Count how many models flag the day as concerning out of total available models. Compute agreementRatio = max(flagCount, modelCount - flagCount) / modelCount. Compute ensembleConfidence = agreementRatio * min(individual component confidences). Map to UncertaintyLevel: >0.8 = .high, >0.5 = .medium, else .low. Add uncertaintyLevel to the daily MLPrediction/InsightResult output struct. In the insight generation logic, only surface insights with .medium or .high confidence. For .low confidence, either suppress the insight or prefix with 'We're not fully certain, but...' This prevents overconfident single-model predictions from alarming users.

tasks.title: Add Monte Carlo Dropout uncertainty for neural network models
tasks.spec: Create MCDropoutInference.swift with a class that runs N stochastic forward passes through a CoreML neural network model. In the TFT model (from train-temporal-fusion-transformer) or the updatable neural net PredictiveScorer model, ensure dropout layers are present in the architecture (add dropout with p=0.1 after each dense layer in the Python training scripts if not already present). In MCDropoutInference: (1) Load the model with MLModelConfiguration where computeUnits = .all. (2) For MC inference, run the same input through the model N=20 times. To keep dropout active during inference, set the model to use a configuration that enables training mode — in practice with CoreML, this requires exporting the model with dropout as a stochastic layer (using coremltools flexible_shape or by keeping the training flag). (3) Collect the N output distributions. (4) Compute mean(outputs) as the point prediction and std(outputs) as the uncertainty estimate. (5) Map to confidence: confidence = 1.0 / (1.0 + standardDeviation). Return MCDropoutResult with (prediction: Double, uncertainty: Double, confidence: Double). Integrate into TFTForecaster: after each forecast call, run MC dropout and attach confidence. Only applicable to neural network models — the logistic regression and tree models skip this.

tasks.title: Add Platt scaling and calibration curves to PredictiveScorer
tasks.spec: In PredictiveScorer.swift, after model training/update, hold out the last 20% of training data as a calibration set. (1) Compute raw logits (pre-sigmoid) for the calibration set. (2) Build a calibration curve: bin predictions into 10 equal-width bins (0-0.1, 0.1-0.2, ..., 0.9-1.0). For each bin, compute mean predicted probability and observed frequency (fraction of actual positives). Store as binAccuracies: [(predictedMean: Double, observedFreq: Double)]. (3) If any bin deviates by more than 0.1 from the diagonal (miscalibrated), apply Platt scaling. Fit P_calibrated = 1/(1+exp(A*logit + B)) on the calibration set by minimizing negative log-likelihood using gradient descent: for 100 iterations, compute gradients dL/dA = sum((p_i - y_i) * logit_i) and dL/dB = sum(p_i - y_i), update A -= lr * dA, B -= lr * dB with lr=0.01. (4) Create a CalibrationState struct with fields: A (Double), B (Double), binAccuracies ([(Double, Double)]), calibrationDate (Date). Store in StoredMLModelState.parametersJSON under key 'calibration'. (5) At inference, pass raw logit through Platt sigmoid before reporting probability. (6) Recalibrate every 30 days alongside model retraining. This ensures reported probabilities are well-calibrated — when the model says 80%, it happens ~80% of the time.
